- If sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4) in recent days, reduce forecasted price spikes; model tends to overreact.
- If sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., > 0.3) and forecast shows a sharp upward move, cap the forecast at 1–2% above recent peak to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment swings sharply (e.g., from +0.3 to -0.5), reduce forecast volatility and shift toward mean-reversion bias.
- If model consistently forecasts higher prices than true outcome in 30-day horizon, apply a 5–10% downward adjustment for the first 5–7 days of the forecast.
- If true outcome shows a sharp drop after a spike, model often overcorrects — reduce forecast slope after peak by 15–20%.
- For sentiment history with high volatility, use a 3-day moving average of sentiment to smooth forecast adjustments.
- If sentiment is consistently low (e.g., < 0.0) over 5+ days, model tends to underestimate — add 3–5% to forecast to compensate for underconfidence.
- Avoid forecasting price increases when sentiment is negative and price is already near 70–72 — model often overestimates recovery.
